Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the United Pacific Insurance Group Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. Instructions for queuing your questions will be given at that time. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to United Pacific Insurance Group's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Jonathan Hale, Chief Executive Officer; Sarah Jenkins, Chief Financial Officer; and Michael Torres, Chief Underwriting Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we are making today may be considered forward-looking. These statements are subject to certain risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those projected. We encourage you to review our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks and uncertainties.

I will now turn the call over to Jonathan Hale.

Jonathan Hale: Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on United Pacific Insurance Group's performance for Q3 2024. We delivered strong results, driven by disciplined underwriting yielding an outstanding combined ratio across all segments, a rock-solid capital position with meaningful surplus growth, robust investment income yields amid favorable rates, and favorable expense ratio trends through operational efficiencies and digital transformation.

Sarah, our CFO, will now provide a more detailed review of our financial performance.

Sarah Jenkins: Thank you, Jonathan, and good morning, everyone. As Jonathan mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Our net income was $320 million, or $2.15 per share. Key drivers of our financial performance included earned premium growth of 8.2%, favorable prior year development, and net investment income up 22% year-over-year. Our combined ratio was 92.3%, reflecting effective underwriting and claims management. We continue to maintain a strong capital position, with consolidated statutory surplus at $8.7 billion and an RBC ratio of 462%.

Let me dive deeper into our combined ratio performance, both overall and by segment, for the third quarter and year-to-date. As a reminder for those new to our calls, the combined ratio is the gold standard metric for underwriting profitability in our industry—it's the sum of our loss ratio, which captures paid and reserved claims divided by earned premiums, and our expense ratio, which includes acquisition costs, underwriting expenses, and other operational overheads divided by earned premiums. A ratio below 100% signals an underwriting profit; above it, a loss. Excluding catastrophe losses and prior year development—or PYD, for short—gives us a cleaner view of underlying trends.

Our overall combined ratio came in at 92.3% for Q3, a 450 basis point improvement from 96.8% in Q3 last year, and year-to-date it's 93.1% versus 97.2% in the prior year. This reflects disciplined underwriting, robust earned premium growth of 8.2% quarter-over-quarter driven by rate adequacy and selective new business, and effective expense management amid persistent inflation pressures. Ex-cat and ex-PYD, the underlying ratio was an even stronger 89.5% in Q3, beating our internal target of 91% and positioning us favorably against peers like Progressive at 91.8% and Travelers at 93.2%, per their recent releases.

Breaking it down, our Q3 loss ratio was 65.2%, down 320 basis points year-over-year, benefiting from lower large loss activity and favorable PYD of $45 million, or 120 basis points of favorability. Cat losses totaled $120 million pre-tax, or 3.2 points on the ratio—primarily from California wildfires and Hurricane Idalia's tail end in the Southeast—still 40% below the five-year Q3 average thanks to our enhanced cat modeling with RMS v18.0 and strategic reinsurance placements via our $2.5 billion tower at Lloyd's and Swiss Re. The expense ratio held steady at 27.1%, a 130 basis point improvement from moderating commission costs on personal lines renewals and our multi-year digital transformation yielding 15% lower policy administration expenses per policy.

Now, let's drill into the segments, where the story gets even more granular. I'll focus on our core property and casualty lines, which represent 85% of earned premiums.

Personal lines, at 42% of our book, delivered a standout 88.7% combined ratio in Q3—up from a stellar 86.2% last quarter but still 510 basis points better than prior year. Earned premiums grew 11% to $1.8 billion, fueled by 6% rate increases on auto and homeowners, plus 200,000 policies from our telematics-based "SafeDrive" program, now live in 28 states with 25% penetration among new customers. Loss ratio was 61.4%, pressured by a 7% uptick in auto severity from repair inflation—think $4,200 average claims, in line with CCC Intelligent Solutions data—but offset by 12% lower frequency via usage-based insurance algorithms partnering with Cambridge Mobile Telematics. Homeowners saw cat-driven losses at 2.8 points, but our AI-powered risk selection reduced exposure in high-WUI zones by 18% year-over-year. Expense ratio ticked up to 27.3% on marketing spend for our bundled "HomePlus Auto" product, targeting millennials with ESG-integrated coverage. Outlook here is bright: We're rolling out generative AI for faster claims triage, aiming for sub-85% underlying by year-end.

Shifting to commercial lines, 35% of premiums, the combined ratio was 95.2%—a 380 basis point improvement and our best Q3 since 2019. Premiums rose 7.5% to $1.5 billion, with middle-market renewals at +9% rates amid hardening markets. Loss ratio improved to 68.1%, thanks to benign workers' comp frequency down 5% per NCCI data and PYD favorability of $30 million from better-than-expected COVID reserve releases. Commercial auto remains a sore spot at 72% loss ratio due to medical inflation and social inflation on litigated claims—our average jury award now $180,000, echoing trends at Chubb—but we've layered in LexisNexis predictive analytics to non-renew 15% of high-risk fleets. General liability saw 1.5 points of cat from Midwest storms, but our parametric trigger products mitigated $20 million in payouts. Expense ratio at 27.1% reflects efficiencies from our Salesforce Einstein implementation, cutting quote cycle times by 40%. Strategically, we're doubling down on SMB expansion via our "UPI Shield" cyber-physical bundle, with early uptake in manufacturing.

Specialty and global operations, our growth engine at 23% of premiums, posted a 96.8% ratio—solid given $80 million in cat losses from European floods and Asia typhoons. Premiums surged 12% to $950 million, led by marine cargo up 15% on supply chain rerouting post-Suez and our D&O book benefiting from M&A rebound. Loss ratio at 69.5% includes 4.2 points ex-US cats, but underlying trends are pristine at 65%, aided by machine learning catastrophe models from AIR Worldwide. In EMEA, our Lloyd's Syndicate 1234 wrote $200 million in aviation, with rates up 10% amid Boeing supply issues. Expense ratio of 27.3% is disciplined, with Asia-Pacific ops leveraging robotic process automation for 20% claims savings. Regionally, U.S. Southeast exposure is capped at 8% of surplus post-reinsurer diversification to Korean Re and SCOR; Europe benefits from our green underwriting incentives, pricing climate-resilient risks 5% lower to attract ESG capital.

Year-to-date trends underscore resilience: Overall earned premiums up 9.1% to $6.2 billion, with rate/net of 7.2% outpacing loss trend of 4.8%. Inflation remains headwind—auto parts +12% year-over-year per BLS, medical +6.5%—but our 2023 pricing actions and 2024 renewals at +8-10% position us well. PYD has been a tailwind, $110 million year-to-date or 180 basis points, reflecting conservative reserving discipline akin to Berkshire Hathaway's approach.

Technically, we're ahead on initiatives: Our "UnderwriteAI" platform, powered by Google Cloud Vertex AI, has boosted quote accuracy 22%, enabling 10% more selective acceptance rates. In catastrophe management, we've stress-tested against 1-in-250 APAC typhoons using FijiBeans open-source models, informing a 15% reinsurance rate cut. Digitally, 65% of policies now issue via mobile app, compressing the expense ratio trajectory toward 25% long-term.

Strategically, this performance funds our $500 million share repurchase and 12% dividend hike announced today. Looking forward, we guide to a full-year underlying combined ratio of 91-93%, with Q4 ex-cat at 90%. Risks include California wildland fire season and potential U.S. litigation reform delays, but tailwinds from rate momentum, UBI scale, and $300 million in tech capex should drive ROE expansion to 14%+. We're not chasing growth at any cost—targeting 8-10% premium CAGR with combined ratios under 92%—mirroring Allstate's pivot but with our superior specialty diversification.

With that foundation on underwriting, let me shift to our capital position and statutory surplus levels. Our balance sheet remains rock-solid, positioning us exceptionally well to navigate the current market dynamics—including elevated catastrophe activity from hurricane season in the Atlantic and inflationary pressures on loss costs across our property and casualty lines.

Our consolidated statutory surplus stood at $8.7 billion as of September 30th, reflecting a robust 14% year-over-year increase and a 6% sequential build from Q2. This growth marks our 17th consecutive quarter of surplus expansion, underscoring the durability of our capital generation engine. Driving this was $1.2 billion in organic surplus growth from underwriting profits and net investment income, partially offset by $450 million in shareholder returns through dividends and share repurchases.

Our risk-based capital ratio remains a standout metric of strength. On a consolidated basis, we're at 462%—well above our internal target range of 400-450% and comfortably exceeding regulatory thresholds under NAIC guidelines. Breaking it down by segment:

Property and casualty: RBC at 478%, up from 455% a year ago. This reflects a statutory surplus of $5.4 billion, bolstered by a 92.8% accident-year combined ratio excluding cats, which generated $850 million in P&C statutory income year-to-date. Cat losses totaled $320 million pre-tax in Q3, primarily from California wildfires and Florida wind events, but our robust reinsurance program—featuring a $2.5 billion excess-of-loss tower with partners like Swiss Re and Munich Re—limited net impact to just 1.2 points on the consolidated combined ratio.

Life and health: RBC at 440%, steady sequentially, with surplus at $2.8 billion. Group life and voluntary benefits drove $210 million in statutory earnings, aided by favorable mortality trends 5% below baseline assumptions. Our term life portfolio, which mirrors products offered by peers like Prudential or MetLife, benefited from higher credited rates amid the Fed's rate hike cycle.

Corporate and other: Surplus of $500 million, supporting group-wide initiatives.

Regionally, our U.S. operations—accounting for 68% of surplus—grew 16% year-over-year, fueled by commercial lines momentum in the Midwest and Southeast industrial sectors. In Europe, our Lloyd's syndicate and direct P&C book added €420 million to surplus, up 11%, despite UK motor pricing softening amid regulatory scrutiny from the FCA. Asia-Pacific, now 12% of total surplus, expanded 22% on strong growth in our Japan auto and China health reinsurance partnerships, though we remain vigilant on earthquake exposure via our industry loss warranty covers.

Turning to trends and drivers, our surplus growth outpaced book value per share accretion of 11%, thanks to $300 million in share repurchases under our $1.5 billion authorization—deploying 65% of our free cash flow target. Investment income contributed meaningfully, with our $45 billion portfolio yielding 4.2% year-to-date, up 80 basis points year-over-year, driven by a 25% allocation to investment-grade corporates and a tactical overweight in municipals amid higher tax-exempt yields. Unrealized gains flipped positive by $180 million in Q3 as duration risk normalized post-rate volatility.

On technical initiatives, we've enhanced our capital management through several key actions. First, our annual ORSA—Own Risk and Solvency Assessment—stress-tested scenarios including a 1-in-200-year U.S. hurricane ($4 billion gross loss) and a 200 basis point parallel yield curve shift, confirming RBC resilience above 350% in all cases. Second, we optimized our reinsurance structure with a 10% increase in ceded premiums to $3.2 billion, achieving collateral efficiency via letters of credit from our $15 billion undrawn lines at JPMorgan and BofA. Third, we're piloting parametric insurance products in Florida and Texas—similar to those rolled out by Lemonade or Swiss Re's digital platforms—to accelerate claims payouts and reduce tail risk.

Strategically, this capital fortress enables disciplined deployment. We've authorized a 12% dividend hike to $0.85 per share, payable next month, with a payout ratio under 35% of statutory earnings—leaving ample dry powder for bolt-on M&A, like our recent $250 million acquisition of a regional workers' comp administrator to densify our E&S platform. Looking ahead, we expect 12-15% surplus growth in 2024, targeting 475%+ consolidated RBC, while maintaining ROE above 15%. Risks remain—persistent social inflation in liability lines and potential NAIC changes to RBC C-3 life risk factors—but our proactive modeling and diversification mitigate these.

Next, on our investment performance, with a particular focus on our investment income yield, which came in at 4.2% for the quarter on a book yield basis—up 110 basis points year-over-year and marking our 10th consecutive quarter of yield expansion. This reflects the ongoing benefits of our disciplined asset-liability management strategy amid a higher-for-longer rate environment. Our running yield—capturing income on assets currently held—ticked up to 4.35%, while new money yields averaged a robust 5.1% on the $2.8 billion we deployed this quarter.

Investment income yield remains a cornerstone of our earnings power here at UPI, especially in our life and annuity segment, where it drives the investment spread—the differential between our portfolio yield and policyholder crediting rates, which averaged 2.8% this quarter for a healthy 142 basis point spread. In our property and casualty book, it bolsters the combined ratio by offsetting underwriting volatility. Overall, investment income contributed $285 million to net income this quarter, a 22% increase from Q3 2023, helping us deliver ROE of 13.2%.

Key drivers start with portfolio composition. Our $45 billion general account portfolio is conservatively positioned: 72% in fixed income, with investment-grade corporates at 45% yielding 4.8% on average, U.S. Treasuries and agencies at 22% yielding 4.1%, and municipals at 12% providing tax-exempt income equivalent to a 5.2% taxable yield. We've tactically trimmed MBS exposure to 8% from 12% last year, rotating into shorter-duration corporate bonds to capture spread widening without extending duration beyond our 5.8-year target, which aligns tightly with our 6.2-year liability duration.

Equities remain at a modest 8%, focused on dividend aristocrats like those in the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats Index, generating a 3.2% dividend yield, while alternatives—including core-plus real estate and infrastructure via funds like Blackstone's BREIT and Brookfield's infrastructure vehicles—make up 12%, delivering a blended 6.4% yield with low correlation to public markets. Credit quality is pristine: 92% rated A or better, with non-investment grade at just 3%, diversified across sectors to avoid concentration risks seen in past cycles, like the 2020 energy downturn.

Year-to-date, yields have expanded from 3.6% at year-end 2023, fueled by the Fed's terminal rate settling around 4.75-5.00% and the Treasury curve steepening—10-year yields up to 4.3% from 3.9% in Q1. This mirrors peers: Allianz reported 4.1% book yield last quarter, while AIG hit 4.5% on aggressive derisking. Our edge comes from proactive reinvestment; since Q4 2022, we've locked in 5.3% new money rates on $12 billion, front-running the rate hike cycle.

Regionally, North America, comprising 65% of our portfolio, yields are strongest at 4.5%, boosted by high-quality RMBS and floating-rate notes tied to SOFR, now averaging Libor + 220 basis points. Europe, at 20% of AUM, lags at 3.7% due to lingering negative real yields in peripherals and ECB rate cuts to 3.5%; we've shifted 15% of euro-denominated holdings into U.S. dollar assets via FX hedges, capturing an extra 80 basis points. Asia-Pacific, our growth engine at 15%, yields 4.0% via JGBs and AUD corporates, but we're monitoring China credit spreads widening post-property sector woes—we've capped exposure there at 2% with opportunistic buys in high-conviction names like Ping An bonds at 5.5%.

We've leaned into several initiatives to sustain this momentum. Our ALM team, using proprietary stochastic modeling with tools like MoSes and Prophet, stress-tested the portfolio under +200 basis point shock scenarios, confirming a 150 basis point cushion to liability costs. We extended our short-duration bucket strategy, targeting 1-3 year bonds yielding 5.0%+, and ramped up private credit allocations to 5% via direct lending partnerships with Ares and Owl Rock, achieving 7.2% net yields with minimal volatility.

On the ESG front, 28% of new investments are SFDR Article 8/9 compliant, blending yield with sustainability—for instance, green bonds from issuers like Ørsted yielding 4.6%. We've also deployed $500 million into catastrophe bonds via our ILS platform, generating 6.8% risk-adjusted yields uncorrelated to rates.

Strategically, we're positioning for a soft landing: expect yields to trough at 4.3-4.5% in 2025 as rates normalize, but our $15 billion maturity wall rolls off at 4.9% blended rates, providing a natural tailwind. We're guiding to full-year book yield of 4.25%, with upside from share repurchases funded by excess capital—our RBC ratio sits at 520% in some views, well above the 400% target.

Risks? Credit migration in a slowdown could pressure spreads, but our 1.5% loan-to-value on commercial real estate and no CLO exposure mitigate that. Compared to Berkshire's float-fueled 3.8% yield, our active management delivers superior results without equity beta.

Finally, on expense ratio trends and drivers, such as commission expenses and operating costs, this came in at 27.1% for Q3, a 130 basis point improvement year-over-year and down from prior periods. This marks one of our best quarterly expense ratios recently, reflecting the tangible impact of our multi-year operational efficiency program, "Zenith Edge." We're on track to deliver our guided range, supported by $175 million in run-rate savings already realized year-to-date.

Breaking it down by key drivers: commissions, which were around 12.1% of earned premiums, down from higher levels a year ago. This moderation was driven by a favorable shift in our product mix toward direct-to-consumer channels, where we now source 42% of our personal lines policies—up from 35% last year—via our Zenith Direct app and partnerships with embedded insurance platforms like those integrated with Uber and Shopify. In our commercial lines, broker commissions ticked up modestly due to higher attachment rates on our new UPI Flex mid-market package product, which saw strong premium growth amid softening commercial rates. Regionally, U.S. commissions held steady, benefiting from our agent portal enhancements that reduced multi-line discounting pressures. In Europe, commissions faced some pressure from Solvency II remuneration caps and increased tied-agent incentives to counter competitive rate cuts from peers like Aviva and Allianz.

Turning to operating costs, at 16.3% of earned premiums—our lowest in five quarters—this reflects aggressive cost levers across the organization. Salaries and benefits, our largest bucket, grew just modestly despite headcount growth in underwriting and claims, thanks to a 15% productivity lift from our AI-powered underwriting engine, enhanced with telematics data from our 5 million connected policyholders. IT and tech spend was controlled as we completed Phase 2 of our cloud migration to AWS, yielding 22% lower data center costs and enabling real-time catastrophe modeling that shaved 10 days off our loss reserve cycles during recent wildfires.

Marketing expenses declined as we optimized our digital ad spend—shifting to performance-based channels like Google Performance Max and Meta Advantage+—driving improvement in customer acquisition cost. Claims adjustment expenses benefited from our GenAI pilot with Guidewire's ClaimCenter, which automated 35% of low-severity auto claims under $5,000, scaled across our large P&C book.

Regionally, our North American segment delivered a strong 27.1% expense ratio, fueled by scale in our homeowners book amid elevated cat activity and reinsurance reforms that stabilized third-party admin costs. EMEA was steady, with motor inflation pushing repair costs up but offset by supply chain efficiencies. In Asia-Pacific, some widening from expansion in India and Indonesia, where we're investing in bancassurance and telematics for micro-insurance, accepting short-term pressure for premium growth.

Strategically, these trends underscore our "Efficiency First" pillar under our 2027 plan, targeting sub-27% long-term through digital distribution scaling to 55% of policies, zero-based budgeting with AI/ML automating 50% of back-office processes, and M&A tuck-ins like our recent regional acquisition adding low-cost specialty lines. Amid headwinds like repair labor inflation up 9% per CCC data, regulatory scrutiny, and global cat losses—these give us an edge over the industry composite.

Looking forward, we expect continued improvement, though vigilant on commission pressures if auto rates soften.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator: Thank you. Instructions for queuing questions: Press star then one on your touchtone phone. Our first question comes from Emily Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Chen: Good morning. Can you provide more color on the catastrophe losses this quarter and how your reinsurance program protected the bottom line?

Jonathan Hale: Good morning, Emily. Thanks for the question. Our cat losses were $120 million pre-tax in Q3, mainly California wildfires and Idalia remnants, but that's 40% below our five-year average. Our $2.5 billion reinsurance tower with Lloyd's, Swiss Re, and others capped the net hit at 3.2 points on the combined ratio. We've also upgraded to RMS v18.0 modeling and stress-tested with FijiBeans for APAC risks, which helped negotiate 15% lower reinsurance rates. Michael, any additional thoughts on underwriting adjustments?

Michael Torres: Absolutely, Jonathan. We've reduced Southeast exposure to 8% of surplus via diversification to Korean Re and SCOR, and our parametric products mitigated $20 million in commercial payouts. This keeps us agile heading into Q4 fire season.

Operator: Our next question comes from David Patel with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Patel: Good morning. Could you discuss the impact of the higher-for-longer rate environment on your investment yield and ALM strategy?

Sarah Jenkins: Good morning, David. The 4.2% book yield, up 110 bps year-over-year, is a direct beneficiary, with new money at 5.1%. We've maintained 5.8-year duration matching our liabilities, trimming MBS to 8% and adding private credit at 7.2% via Ares. Our stochastic modeling with MoSes confirms resilience to shocks, and cat bonds add uncorrelated 6.8% yield. We're guiding full-year 4.25%, with the $15 billion maturity wall rolling at 4.9%.

Operator: Our next question comes from Lisa Wong with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Lisa Wong: Thanks. On expense trends, how sustainable is the 27.1% level with ongoing tech investments?

Sarah Jenkins: Great question, Lisa. The Zenith Edge program has locked in $175 million savings, with AWS migration cutting data costs 22% and GenAI automating 35% of small claims. Commissions moderated via 42% direct channel mix, and we're targeting sub-27% by 2027 with 55% digital policies. Short-term Asia expansion adds pressure, but long-term levers like zero-based budgeting keep us ahead of peers.

Operator: Our next question from Robert Kline with Barclays.

Robert Kline: Morning, team. Thoughts on capital deployment—any larger M&A on the horizon beyond tuck-ins?

Jonathan Hale: Robert, our $8.7 billion surplus and 462% RBC give us flexibility. We've done $300 million repurchases and the $250 million workers' comp deal, but we're eyeing bolt-ons in E&S and cyber to leverage our specialty strength. Dividend up 12% to $0.85, payout under 35%. No rush—discipline first.

Operator: Our final question from Maria Gonzalez with Deutsche Bank.

Maria Gonzalez: Good morning. How are you positioning personal lines for auto severity inflation?

Michael Torres: Morning, Maria. Auto severity up 7% to $4,200 average per CCC data, but frequency down 12% via SafeDrive telematics with Cambridge Mobile, now 25% new customer penetration. Non-renewing high-risk via LexisNexis, and GenAI claims triage rolling out. Expecting sub-85% underlying by year-end.

Operator: Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session.

Jonathan Hale: Thank you for your questions and your interest in United Pacific Insurance Group. In closing, we are confident in our ability to continue delivering strong results and creating value for our shareholders, backed by underwriting excellence, capital strength, yield discipline, and efficiency gains. Thank you for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
